findings.quote: a spectral line of hydrogen has a wavelength of $600$ nm
findings.problem: Example #2 states a false fact about hydrogen. Hydrogen has no spectral line near 600 nm. Its visible lines are at about 656.3, 486.1, 434.0, 410.2 and 397.0 nm (the red line is 656.3 nm). A student who keeps this stem as a fact learns a wrong wavelength for hydrogen. The illustration marker before 'This rule has limits' repeats the same 600 nm hydrogen line. The arithmetic of the example (z = 0.1) is right; the named element and wavelength are not. This was not raised in round 1.
findings.source: NIST Handbook of Basic Atomic Spectroscopic Data, Hydrogen, strong lines in air (physics.nist.gov/PhysRefData/Handbook/Tables/hydrogentable2.htm): 6562.71, 4861.29, 4340.46, 4101.74, 3970.07 angstroms, nothing near 6000 angstroms; content-checklist.md B01
